p.x:
One day, Nok found a wallet on the street. Inside, there was a lot of money. Her friend said, "Keep it! Nobody will know." But Nok didn't want to be greedy.
She knew that keeping the money was not right. She took the wallet to the police station. The next day, the owner, an old man, called her. He said, "Thank you for telling the truth. Most people would keep it."
Nok's friend felt bad. "I'm sorry," she said. "Please forgive me." Nok smiled. "It's OK. But it's unfair to take other people's money. And it's cruel to the person who lost it." Nok believes everyone has the freedom to choose to do the right thing.

Every day, we make choices about what is good and bad. Most of us learn our values from our families, schools and religions. For example, many people believe that stealing is a sin and that we should treat everyone with equality, whatever their background.
But moral questions are not always simple. Imagine your friend has a terrible haircut and asks your opinion. Do you tell the truth or tell a white lie to protect her feelings? Many people think a small lie that causes no harm is acceptable. Others disagree. It depends on your point of view.
Sometimes doing the right thing takes courage. If you see someone being bullied, will you speak up or stay silent? It is easy to blame others for not helping, but harder to act ourselves. People who help strangers without expecting anything back are often described as selfless. Everyone has human rights, and we should stand up for people who are treated unfairly, even when the temptation to stay silent is strong. Fighting prejudice and discrimination starts with small actions, and people of integrity act on principle, guided by their conscience and a sense of justice.
Thinking about these questions helps us understand ourselves. Stories and fables often end with a moral, a lesson about how to behave. The fact that people from different cultures often reach similar answers suggests that some values may be shared by all humans.

Philosophers have argued about ethics for thousands of years, but modern science has created new dilemmas that earlier thinkers could never have imagined. Gene editing, for example, may one day allow doctors to remove inherited diseases before a child is born. Supporters say it would reduce enormous suffering; critics fear it could lead to "designer babies" and new forms of inequality. Similarly, animal testing has contributed to many medical breakthroughs, yet many people consider it immoral to cause animals pain, even for human benefit.
At the end of life, too, ethical questions are unavoidable. Euthanasia is legal in a small number of countries, where supporters argue that terminally ill patients should be allowed to die with dignity. Opponents worry that vulnerable people could feel pressured to end their lives.
Many ethical debates involve a conflict between individual rights and the greater good. Can a government justify limiting personal freedom to protect public health? Is it acceptable to break a promise if doing so prevents serious harm? Our answers often depend not only on the consequences of an action but also on the motive behind it.
Ethics is not only about large public issues. In everyday life, people face smaller tests: whether to turn a blind eye when a colleague behaves unethically, or whether to act when they witness something wrong. Psychologists have found that a bystander is less likely to help if many other people are present, as each assumes someone else will act. Courage, honesty and compassion have been regarded as a virtue in almost every society, yet practising them is rarely easy.
